planting.note: Direct sow after soil reaches 65F; the short-season breeding makes it useful as a quick spring or late-summer catch crop between longer-season southern peas.

directions: Bred by Carol Deppe in Oregon specifically to mature fast in cool Pacific Northwest summers, this compact, bushy southern pea handles Gulf South heat well despite its cool-climate breeding origin, making it a good fast-maturing choice for a spring or late-summer planting window. Plants are semi-erect and bear 7-8 inch yellow pods that are easy to pick and shell by hand. The small white 'lady pea' type seed cooks quickly without soaking, a real advantage for a fast weeknight side dish in zone 9 summer heat.

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil once reliably warm, exactly as with standard crowder-type southern peas.

directions: Released by USDA-ARS in 2002 as a direct replacement for the classic Alabama 'Knuckle Purple Hull,' bred to add resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus and root-knot nematode, both serious limiters of cowpea yield in sandy Gulf Coast soil. Pods are slightly curved, roughly 8 inches long, purple-hulled, holding about 14 smaller, smooth brown peas per pod, with seed running noticeably smaller than the old-line strain. Expect similar yield to the original Knuckle Purple Hull but with meaningfully better performance where nematodes have historically been a problem.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service variety release notice (Fery, Thies and Gillaspie, 2002)

planting.note: Direct sow with a trellis or ample room to sprawl; this type is strongly daylength-sensitive and won't bulk up its main pod flush until day length shrinks back toward 13 hours in late summer, so don't expect an early harvest.

directions: A pre-1940 South Carolina heirloom collected in 1992 and now maintained by USDA-ARS in Charleston, about as regionally Gulf and Southeast-pedigreed as a cowpea gets. Vigorous 10-15 foot sprawling or climbing vines need a trellis or plenty of room, producing a big flush of 9-inch pods in late summer into fall rather than early in the season. The gray-and-tan speckled seed carries good resistance to root-knot nematode, and seed coats are selected to be permeable enough that volunteers don't survive winter, a useful 'won't become a weed' trait.
sources: USDA-ARS Plant Germplasm System (Charleston, SC maintenance records)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; cage or stake at transplant since determinate plants still need support once loaded with fruit, and irrigate consistently to avoid blossom-end rot.

directions: Listed by LSU AgCenter among determinate, heat-tolerant tomatoes carrying tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) resistance, the thrips-vectored virus that is one of the biggest headaches for Gulf Coast tomato growers. As a determinate, bush-habit hybrid it suits a compressed, cage-supported spring crop timed to set fruit before peak July-August heat, with a second planting possible for fall. TSWV resistance reduces but doesn't eliminate thrips-management needs, so reflective mulch is still worthwhile in zone 9 gardens.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; stake or cage at transplant and irrigate consistently to avoid blossom-end rot in uneven Gulf Coast summer soil moisture.

directions: Appears alongside Tribeca on the same LSU AgCenter recommended list, determinate, heat-tolerant, and TSWV-resistant, making it one of the extension service's standard picks for a Louisiana or Gulf South spring tomato crop that needs to keep setting fruit as nights stay warm. Treat it as a direct substitute or companion planting for other heat-set determinate slicers if you want to compare performance side by side in your own yard. Consistent irrigation through fruit set matters more than fertility for avoiding cracking and blossom-end rot in this type.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; plan a second planting 3-4 weeks later for continuous summer harvest rather than relying on one big flush.

directions: Listed by LSU AgCenter as heat-tolerant with Alternaria and Fusarium race 1/2 resistance, this variety was originally popularized as a heat-set performer for the arid Southwest, but the same ability to set fruit when days top 90F and nights stay above 75F makes it valuable for the Gulf South's humid-heat fruit-set problem, not just dry heat. It's a determinate, medium-fruited red slicer around 7 ounces that produces a concentrated harvest window. Stake it at transplant and keep irrigation steady through fruit set.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost into cages or stakes; expect strong performance against Gray Leaf Spot, a foliar disease that thrives in Gulf Coast humidity.

directions: A 1997 joint release from NC State's Mountain Horticultural Crops station and the University of Florida's Bradenton research center, bred collaboratively for fresh-market performance across the hot, humid Southeast. LSU AgCenter lists it heat-tolerant with resistance to Fusarium races 1-3 and Gray Leaf Spot. Fruits run medium at 8-10 ounces, round, and red on a determinate plant, filling the same summer heat-set niche as other recommended determinate slicers and worth trialing side by side if disease pressure in a given yard differs from the standard package.

planting.note: Direct sow in late winter for spring, or in early fall while still hot; in zone 9a, afternoon shade during the final weeks before harvest extends the usable window.

directions: A Batavian summer-crisp type bred specifically to hold quality through heat, rated tolerant of bolting, tipburn, and bottom rot, and carrying resistance to downy mildew and lettuce mosaic virus, which matters in Gulf South humidity. The red-tipped, thick, crisp leaves stay sweet rather than turning bitter as temperatures climb, and at a fast 48 days it can squeeze in before spring heat sets in or go in for an early-fall planting while still hot. It makes a strong companion or rotation choice alongside other heat-tolerant Batavian lettuces.
